accuracy.reason: Copies-and-purpose, asynchronous-ack and synchronous-ack correctly scope read capacity, loss windows and stage/count-dependent guarantees. Primary PostgreSQL docs confirm received, durable and replayed are distinct.

evidence.quote: Nor does every synchronous mode guarantee that replica reads already show the change.

mechanisms.reason: Copy-then-changes teaches matching snapshot/log boundary and ordered application. Lag-and-read-routing, safe-failover and copies-versus-history explain visibility evidence, authority fencing and restoration rather than topology slogans.

evidence.quote: The initial copy and starting log position must agree.

coherence.reason: All nine objectives build from copy propagation to acknowledgement, lag, write arrangements, takeover, history and policy. Prerequisites suffice; assigned diagrams accurately distinguish receive/apply and show a scoped safe failover sequence. Shared assets inspected, not UI-tested.

evidence.quote: A missing response does not prove the old leader stopped.

decisions.reason: Write-arrangements and choose-guarantees connect each extra writable copy to conflict work, and each durability/freshness promise to latency, unavailable acknowledgements and recovery costs.

evidence.quote: Choose acceptable acknowledged-write loss, read freshness, write latency and recovery time before choosing replica settings.

clarity.reason: Terms are introduced with operational meanings and profile/failover examples expose concrete consequences. No unexplained numeric guarantee or unsupported fixed-delay freshness promise.

evidence.quote: A fixed sleep or low average lag is not proof that a particular write is visible.

outcomes.reason: All six criteria supported across the learner: copies versus subsets, read/recovery routing, no automatic throughput/continuity, matching copy/log handoff, source order and receipt versus query-visible application. Storage/coordination work is explicit in the final policy answer.

All seven criteria supported: configured acknowledgement, avoided remote wait, permanent-primary-loss trace, required set/count and stage, durable versus applied, missing confirmation stalls and bounded failure protection.

All eight criteria supported: stage-sensitive lag, read-your-writes, primary versus specific application wait and their costs, acceptable stale reads, no fixed-sleep/lost-write rescue, and all three writer topologies with explicit conflict/repair obligations.

All seven criteria supported: promotion and uncertain failure, suitable current candidate, fencing before replacement authority, application reconnection, propagated deletion, retained historical recovery and measured usable restore. The proposed policy explicitly exercises takeover and routing.

All four criteria supported: learner asks for loss/freshness/latency/recovery targets, proposes monitored report replicas plus durable confirmations, specifies protected takeover and backups/tests, and retains network/storage/operational and failure-scope limits.

sourceChecks.claim: Live RDS read-replica documentation describes read-only copies and routing queries to scale read-heavy work, not automatic write scaling or failover.
Live PostgreSQL Logical Replication describes initial snapshot, subsequent ordered changes and logical identity versus physical byte copying, supporting the coordinated copy/change handoff.
Live PostgreSQL warm standby explicitly warns asynchronous shipping can lose committed transactions on catastrophic primary failure and that replica visibility lags.

Live PostgreSQL synchronous replication explains selected standby counts, durable receipt versus remote_write and remote_apply, increased response time and potentially blocked commits when confirmations are unavailable.
Live MySQL WAIT_FOR_EXECUTED_GTID_SET waits for application of specified transactions and reports timeout, directly supporting progress evidence rather than fixed sleep.

Live Cassandra Dynamo documentation describes coordinator-to-replica writes, configured acknowledgement counts, last-write-wins and repair. PostgreSQL and Brewer followups verify single-leader and independently writable conflict consequences.

Live PostgreSQL Failover requires preventing two servers both believing they are primary, discusses STONITH, external failure detection and address migration. This verifies separate authority and routing work.

Live PostgreSQL continuous archiving describes base backup plus continuous retained WAL and stopping at a recovery point; this verifies why replicated current state and historical recovery differ and why retained logs matter.

Live Brewer partition-recovery article supports operation-dependent availability/conflict policy; checked PostgreSQL synchronous, failover and recovery sections substantiate the explicit latency/loss/recovery tradeoffs and testing needs.
